القاهرة، الاثنين 2 نوفمبر 2026، اجتماعات مصرية سودانية رفيعة المستوى بصيغة «2+2»، تضم وزيري الخارجية والموارد المائية والري في البلدين، في تحرك دبلوماسي يعكس أهمية التنسيق بين دولتي المصب بشأن القضايا المشتركة. وتأتي الاجتماعات في وقت تواجه فيه العلاقات الإقليمية المرتبطة بنهر النيل تحديات معقدة، أبرزها استمرار الخلاف بشأن سد النهضة الإثيوبي، وتداعيات الحرب في السودان، والحاجة إلى تعزيز التعاون الفني لإدارة الموارد المائية. أخبار متعلقة بين صمود الرفض المصري والمخطط الإثيوبي.. إلى أين تتجه أزمة النيل؟ افتتاح سد إثيوبي جديد يهدد مصر.. أين الحقيقة وراء طمأنة الحصص المائية؟ السيسي يوجه رسالة حازمة لدول حوض النيل: لا تفريط في الأمن المائي وبحسب جدول الاجتماعات المعلن، يعقد وزير الخارجية المصري بدر عبد العاطي لقاءً ثنائيًا مع نظيره السوداني، يعقبه اجتماع رباعي يضم وزيري الري، إلى جانب مباحثات موسعة بمشاركة وفدي البلدين. سد النهضة.. ملف لم يُغلق رغم انتهاء جولات التفاوض السابقة دون التوصل إلى اتفاق ملزم بشأن قواعد ملء وتشغيل سد النهضة، فإن الخلاف حول إدارة مياه النيل لا يزال يمثل أحد الملفات الاستراتيجية في العلاقات بين مصر والسودان وإثيوبيا. وكانت مصر قد أعلنت في ديسمبر 2023 انتهاء المسار التفاوضي آنذاك دون نتائج، في ظل استمرار الخلافات بشأن القواعد المنظمة لتشغيل السد والتعامل مع فترات الجفاف. وتؤكد القاهرة أهمية التوصل إلى ترتيبات قانونية وفنية تضمن حماية مصالح دول المصب، بينما تتمسك إثيوبيا بحقها في الاستفادة من السد لتوليد الكهرباء وتحقيق التنمية. وتكتسب المشاورات المصرية السودانية أهمية خاصة باعتبار أن البلدين يتشاركان مصالح مباشرة في انتظام تدفقات النيل، وإن اختلفت بعض الاعتبارات الفنية والاقتصادية المرتبطة بالسد. تنسيق فني لحماية المنشآت المائية شهدت الاتصالات بين مسؤولي الري في البلدين بحث عدد من ملفات التعاون الفني، وفي مقدمتها تبادل البيانات الهيدرولوجية ومتابعة تدفقات المياه. وتكتسب هذه البيانات أهمية كبيرة في تشغيل السدود والخزانات السودانية والسد العالي في مصر، فضلًا عن تحسين الاستعداد للتعامل مع التغيرات المفاجئة في مستويات المياه. كما شملت مباحثات التعاون ملفات حماية المنشآت المائية ومآخذ مياه الشرب والري خلال مواسم الفيضان، وتأهيل بعض المنشآت السودانية، ومنها خزان جبل الأولياء. وتبرز هذه القضايا أهمية التعاون العملي بين القاهرة والخرطوم، بعيدًا عن المواقف السياسية وحدها، بالنظر إلى الترابط الجغرافي والهيدرولوجي بين البلدين. الحرب السودانية وتعقيدات الأمن المائي لا يمكن فصل التعاون المصري السوداني عن الظروف التي يعيشها السودان نتيجة الحرب المستمرة وتداعياتها على مؤسسات الدولة والبنية التحتية. فإدارة الموارد المائية تحتاج إلى أجهزة فنية قادرة على جمع البيانات، وصيانة المنشآت، ومتابعة تشغيل الخزانات، وتنسيق الإجراءات مع الجهات المختصة في دول الجوار. وتفرض الأوضاع السودانية تحديات إضافية تتعلق بقدرة المؤسسات على أداء هذه الوظائف بكفاءة واستمرارية. كما أن استقرار السودان يمثل مصلحة استراتيجية لمصر، بالنظر إلى امتداد الحدود المشتركة، والتداخل الاقتصادي والاجتماعي، وأهمية التنسيق بشأن مياه النيل. هل تعود المفاوضات مع إثيوبيا؟ لا يعني عقد الاجتماعات الثنائية بين القاهرة والخرطوم بالضرورة الإعلان عن جولة تفاوض جديدة مع إثيوبيا. لكن تعزيز التنسيق بين دولتي المصب قد يساعد في بلورة مواقف مشتركة بشأن إدارة النهر، وتبادل المعلومات، والتعامل مع التطورات المرتبطة بالسد الإثيوبي. ويظل أي استئناف رسمي للمفاوضات مرتبطًا بإعلانات الأطراف المعنية، وبوجود إطار تفاوضي واضح وأجندة محددة. ومن ثم فإن أهمية الاجتماعات الحالية لا تتوقف على احتمال استئناف المفاوضات، وإنما تمتد إلى قدرة البلدين على تطوير آليات عملية للتعاون المائي. ما الذي يمكن أن تحققه الاجتماعات؟ تتعدد الملفات التي يمكن أن تمثل نتائج ملموسة للتنسيق المصري السوداني، وفي مقدمتها انتظام تبادل البيانات، وتعزيز التعاون الفني، ودعم المؤسسات المسؤولة عن إدارة المياه، وتطوير آليات الاستعداد للفيضانات. كما تتيح اللقاءات فرصة لتنسيق الرؤى الدبلوماسية بشأن القضايا الإقليمية المرتبطة بحوض النيل، في ظل استمرار التحديات المتعلقة بالأمن المائي. غير أن الحكم على نتائج هذه التحركات يتطلب انتظار البيانات الرسمية الختامية، ومعرفة ما إذا كانت الاجتماعات ستسفر عن ترتيبات تنفيذية جديدة أو اتفاقات محددة. بين الدبلوماسية وواقع الأمن المائي تؤكد الاجتماعات المصرية السودانية أن ملف مياه النيل يظل أحد الثوابت الاستراتيجية في العلاقات بين البلدين، وأن التنسيق بشأنه يتجاوز حدود اللقاءات الدبلوماسية المعتادة. لكن الاختبار الحقيقي سيكون في مدى قدرة الطرفين على تحويل التفاهمات السياسية إلى تعاون فني مستدام، والتعامل مع التداعيات المائية والإقليمية في ظل الظروف الراهنة. ويبقى السؤال المطروح: هل تنجح القاهرة والخرطوم في بناء موقف أكثر تنسيقًا تجاه تحديات النيل، أم تظل أزمة سد النهضة مفتوحة دون تسوية نهائية؟ شارك: واتساب فيسبوك إكس تيليجرام ومعالجة الاختلالات المرتبطة بتوريد حصائل الصادر. وناقش الاجتماع أبرز المشكلات التي تواجه المصدرين وسبل معالجتها، إلى جانب تعزيز كفاءة الإجراءات والضوابط المنظمة للقطاع، بما يحقق التوازن بين المصلحة العامة للدولة ومصالح المنتجين والمصدرين، ويسهم في زيادة عائدات الصادر وتعظيم الاستفادة من موارد البلاد من النقد الأجنبي. وتصدرت قضايا تسعير الذهب مداولات الاجتماع، الذي بحث ضرورة تطوير آلية مرنة وعادلة للتسعير تستند إلى الأسعار العالمية، بما يضمن تحقيق عوائد مجزية للدولة والبنك المركزي والشركات والمصدرين. كما تناول مراجعة سقوف التحويلات والقيود المفروضة على تحويلات حصائل الصادر، بهدف تيسير الإجراءات وتحسين انسياب النقد الأجنبي عبر القنوات الرسمية. وبحث المشاركون أهمية تنويع أسواق تصدير الذهب السوداني وفتح وجهات جديدة، لتوسيع فرص النفاذ إلى الأسواق الخارجية وتقليل مخاطر الاعتماد على أسواق محدودة، فضلاً عن تعزيز القدرة التفاوضية للصادرات السودانية. وفيما يتعلق بالسياسات والتشريعات، أكد الاجتماع أهمية مراجعة وتطوير الأطر التنظيمية والقانونية، ووضع حزمة من السياسات والحوافز معالجات تحقق التوازن بين متطلبات المصلحة العامة ومصالح المصدرين، وتؤسس لبيئة استثمارية وتنظيمية مستقرة ومحفزة. كما شددت على ضرورة دعم وتمكين الشباب العاملين في مجال تصدير الذهب، باعتبارهم شريحة فاعلة في مستقبل القطاع، معربة عن تقديرها لجهود الهيئة السودانية للمواصفات والمقاييس في تسهيل إجراءات الصادر وتعزيز الرقابة. من جانبه، أكد وزير المعادن نور الدائم طه دعمه لسياسات بنك السودان المركزي والجهود الرامية إلى تنظيم قطاع صادر الذهب، مشيراً إلى حرص الوزارة على التنسيق المستمر مع البنك والعمل المشترك لتذليل العقبات التي تواجه المنتجين والمصدرين. وفي سياق متصل، انتقد الأمين العام لشعبة مصدري الذهب، للجهات الرسمية، ووضع خبراتها السابقة الناجحة في مجال صادر الذهب تحت تصرف البنك المركزي والجهات ذات الصلة. ويمثل الذهب أحد أهم مصادر النقد الأجنبي للاقتصاد السوداني، في ظل تراجع الصادرات الأخرى وتزايد الضغوط على موارد البلاد من العملات الأجنبية، كما يواجه القطاع تحديات مرتبطة بعمليات التهريب، وتعدد قنوات الشراء والتصدير، ومدى جاذبية الأسعار والإجراءات الرسمية مقارنة بالأسواق الخارجية. الكلمات: الهجمات بالطائرات المسيّرة على البنية التحتية الحيوية للطاقة في السودان، مما تسبب في انقطاع واسع النطاق للكهرباء وتعطيل الخدمات الأساسية وإمدادات المياه النظيفة، فيما يواصل السكان الفرار من ديارهم بحثا عن الأمان. وفي مؤتمره الصحفي اليومي، نقل ستيفان دوجاريك المتحدث باسم الأمين العام، قلق مكتب الأمم المتحدة لتنسيق الشؤون الإنسانية (أوتشا) إزاء هذه الهجمات وتداعياتها على السكان في عدد من الولايات السودانية. وبحسب التقارير، استهدفت غارات بطائرات مسيّرة اليوم محطتين لتوليد الكهرباء في ولاية كسلا، ومحطة فرعية في مروي. وطالت هجمات أمس مرافق كهربائية في ولاية نهر النيل، فيما استُهدفت يوم السبت محطة فرعية في ولاية البحر الأحمر، إلى جانب مواقع في شمال كردفان وولاية الجزيرة. تعطل المياه النظيفة ومخاطر انتشار الأمراض وأكد شركاء الأمم المتحدة في العمل الإنساني أن انقطاع الكهرباء ونقص الوقود أديا إلى تعطل إمدادات المياه النظيفة، مما اضطر السكان إلى الاعتماد على مصادر مياه غير معالجة، وهو ما يزيد من مخاطر الإصابة بالأمراض المنقولة عبر المياه. وأشار دوجاريك إلى أن الهجمات لا تزال مستمرة، وأشار إلى إدانة الأمين العام الشديدة لتصاعد هجمات المسيّرات التي تنفذها أطراف النزاع. وكان الأمين العام قد ذكر، في بيان صدر قبل يومين ، أن هذه الهجمات تسببت في مقتل مئات المدنيين، بينهم نساء وأطفال، في أنحاء السودان ومنطقة أبيي، في انتهاك صارخ للقانون الدولي الإنساني. وأعرب عن استيائه البالغ إزاء الهجمات التي تستهدف المدنيين والبنية التحتية الحيوية التي يعتمدون عليها، بما فيها المرافق الصحية. ودعا الأطراف إلى الاتفاق فورا على وقف الأعمال العدائية والانخراط بحسن نية في جهود الوساطة، بما فيها الجهود التي يقودها مبعوثه الشخصي للسودان، بيكا هافيستو. استمرار النزوح في دارفور والنيل الأزرق وفي شمال دارفور، يواصل السكان الفرار من ديارهم بحثا عن الأمان. وتقدّر المنظمة الدولية للهجرة أن نحو ألفي شخص نزحوا من قريتي كانو وبارو خلال الأسبوع الماضي. أما في ولاية النيل الأزرق، فقد نزح ما يقرب من 120 ألف رجل وامرأة وطفل بين كانون الثاني/يناير ومنتصف الشهر الماضي. وجدد المتحدث باسم الأمين العام الدعوة إلى حماية المدنيين واحترام القانون الدولي الإنساني، والسماح للعاملين في المجال الإنساني بإيصال المساعدات حيثما ومتى تشتد الحاجة إليها. هافيستو يعتزم العودة إلى السودان وعلى صعيد الجهود الدبلوماسية، أفاد دوجاريك بأن بيكا هافيستو اختتم أمس زيارة استغرقت يومين إلى المنامة في البحرين، شارك خلالها في "حوار المنامة" الذي نظمه المعهد الدولي للدراسات الاستراتيجية. وعقد هافيستو على هامش الحوار لقاءات مع عدد من المسؤولين، بينهم وزير خارجية البحرين. وجاءت الزيارة عقب مشاركته الأسبوع الماضي في منتدى أديس أبابا والاجتماع السنوي للمبعوثين الإقليميين إلى منطقة القرن الأفريقي. ويعتزم هافيستو العودة إلى السودان خلال الأسابيع المقبلة لمواصلة التواصل مع الأطراف المعنية الرئيسية، بما فيها السلطات السودانية، لبحث ethiopia.content: East Africa: Ethiopia's Defence Modernization Signals New Era of Strategic Deterrence - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français East Africa: Ethiopia's Defence Modernization Signals New Era of Strategic Deterrence 1 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) By Staff Writer Ethiopia's announcement of the acquisition of advanced Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets and plans to receive S-400 air defence systems marks a significant development in the country's efforts to modernize its national defence capabilities, strengthen the protection of its airspace and reinforce its strategic deterrence. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced on October 28 in Moscow, Russia that Ethiopia had taken delivery of its first batch of Su-35 fighter jets under an agreement with Russia and would also receive four batteries of the S-400 air defence system. He described the development as a major milestone in the country's efforts to strengthen national security, safeguard sovereignty and contribute to regional stability. The announcement, made during the Prime Minister's visit to Moscow for the Third Russia-Africa Summit, also underscored the growing defence cooperation between Ethiopia and Russia. Beyond Military Acquisition: A Strategic Investment in National Security Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The acquisition represents more than the addition of advanced military equipment to Ethiopia's arsenal. It reflects a broader effort to build a modern defence force capable of responding to evolving security challenges and protecting the country's national interests. The Su-35, a fourth-generation-plus multirole fighter, is designed to undertake air-superiority and air-to-ground missions. Its advanced radar, manoeuvrability and weapons systems provide capabilities for airspace surveillance, interception and a range of combat operations. The planned acquisition of the Russian-made S-400 system would add another dimension to Ethiopia's air defence architecture. Designed to engage aircraft, cruise missiles and other aerial threats, the system is intended to provide long-range air defence capabilities and strengthen the protection of strategic assets. Together, these platforms could expand Ethiopia's capacity to monitor and defend its airspace. However, their effectiveness will depend not only on the equipment itself but also on trained personnel, maintenance systems, logistics, command-and-control infrastructure and the ability to integrate different defence capabilities. Deterrence as an Instrument of Peace The strategic significance of military modernization extends beyond battlefield capabilities. A credible defence posture can serve as a deterrent by raising the potential costs of aggression and discouraging threats before they escalate into conflict. Prime Minister Abiy has emphasized this principle, noting that military preparedness is not simply about fighting wars but also about preventing them. For Ethiopia, strengthening defence readiness is closely connected to protecting its sovereignty, territorial integrity and national development interests. The objective, as articulated by the government, is to build the capacity to safeguard peace and security while reducing vulnerability to external threats. This approach places deterrence within a broader national security framework in which military preparedness is intended to support stability rather than confrontation. Regional Security and the Horn of Africa Ethiopia's defence modernization carries significance beyond its national borders, particularly given its strategic position in the Horn of Africa and its extensive economic and security interests across the wider Red Sea region. As a landlocked country with a large population and substantial dependence on regional trade and transport corridors, Ethiopia has important interests in the security of its airspace, critical infrastructure and cross-border economic connections. The evolving security environment in the Horn of Africa, together with the growing use of drones, precision-guided weapons and other emerging military technologies, has increased the importance of modern surveillance, air defence and rapid-response capabilities. In this context, Ethiopia's investment in advanced fighter aircraft and air defence systems reflects an effort to adapt its defence posture to changing regional and technological realities. At the same time, military modernization alone cannot guarantee regional stability. Sustainable peace also requires diplomatic engagement, confidence-building, respect for national sovereignty and stronger regional cooperation. A credible deterrent is most effective when complemented by constructive relations with neighbouring countries and regional institutions. Building a Modern and Sustainable Defence Force The acquisition of advanced platforms also places greater importance on the institutional and technological foundations of national defence. Operating sophisticated fighter aircraft and integrated air defence systems requires specialized training, reliable maintenance facilities, technical expertise, secure supply chains and sustained investment in personnel development. The Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) has made significant strides in expanding its military capabilities through the acquisition of modern and sophisticated weaponry, reflecting an ambitious effort to transform its defence posture. Beyond conventional military capabilities, the ENDF is increasingly moving towards a technology-driven defence model, seeking to integrate artificial intelligence, cyber operations, digital warfare and advanced surveillance technologies into its military operations. This transition reflects the changing nature of modern warfare, where technological superiority, real-time intelligence and integrated command-and-control systems are becoming increasingly important. However, building a modern and technologically advanced military requires more than acquiring sophisticated weapons systems. It also demands sustained investment in specialized training, technical expertise, maintenance infrastructure, logistics, research and development, and institutional capacity to operate and sustain these capabilities over the long term. Strengthening these foundations will be essential to translating military modernization into lasting operational readiness and strategic self-reliance. Building such capabilities is essential to ensuring that military modernization translates into sustainable national defence readiness. The delivery of the Su-35 fighter jets and the planned arrival of the S-400 systems signal an expansion of the country's defence ambitions and its military cooperation with Russia. Ultimately, the significance of this modernization will be measured not simply by the sophistication of the equipment acquired, but by the country's ability to translate those capabilities into effective national defence, strategic resilience and a more secure regional environment. Thomas Fleurine Sorensen, Counsellor at the Embassy of Denmark in Ethiopia, highlighted the longstanding partnership between the two countries during an interview with ENA on the sidelines of the Third Ethiopian Water and Energy Week in Addis Ababa. He said Ethiopia's progress in renewable energy and its commitment to sustainable development provide a strong foundation for expanding bilateral cooperation, particularly through knowledge exchange, institutional partnerships, and greater private-sector engagement. Sorensen identified the Assela Wind Farm as a flagship example of the two countries' cooperation. He particularly highlighted the importance of science-based, evidence-driven policymaking in the energy sector. Commending Ethiopia's achievements in expanding its electricity grid and advancing universal energy access, the diplomat said the country's experience offers valuable lessons for other African nations pursuing ambitious energy and development targets. With Ethiopia preparing to host COP32 in 2027, Sorensen also stressed the importance of strategic planning and clear priorities in advancing the country's climate ambitions, reaffirming Denmark's readiness to support its global climate objectives. Undersecretary of the Ministry of Culture, Information and Tourism Dr Graham Abdel-Gadir said in a press statement that the Council discussed the latest developments in the country and condemned the repeated attacks on service facilities and infrastructure using drones launched from within Ethiopia, describing them as crimes against humanity. He said the Council stressed the need to raise the state of alert to the highest level, both officially and among the public. It also directed that all conspiracies being plotted against the country be monitored and that the maximum possible penalties be imposed on anyone proven to have supplied the enemy with coordinates of strategic and civilian sites. The Undersecretary added that the Cabinet considered the targeting of civilian service facilities an indication of the successive defeats suffered by the rebel Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia. He noted that the Cabinet had directed the coordination and organisation of media campaigns inside and outside the country, involving institutions, ministries and individuals, to condemn the repeated attacks by the rebel militia and its supporters. The Undersecretary explained that the Cabinet had directed that protection be strengthened for facilities, power stations and their personnel at both the federal and state levels. Dr Graham Abdel-Gadir also noted that the Cabinet reviewed a report on the supply of petroleum products. Minister of Energy Engineer Al-Motasem Ibrahim indicated that nine vessels were available, in addition to three more vessels imported by the Sudanese Petroleum Corporation, carrying a combined total of 120,000 tonnes. He added that the Council heard a report from the Ministry of Industry and Trade on its efforts to ensure the availability of essential commodities. It also reviewed ongoing efforts to rehabilitate bridges in Khartoum State, particularly Shambat, Halfaya and Al-Dabasin bridges. ethiopia.content: Security In The Red Sea and The Case for an Inclusive Maritime Order – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-11-02 Security In The Red Sea and The Case for an Inclusive Maritime Order 0 Comments The Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden constitute a strategic nexus connecting the Mediterranean, the Indian Ocean and the wider global trading system. Their security is consequently inseparable from the stability of the Horn of Africa, the institutional capacity of neighbouring states and the resilience of international supply chains. Disruptions to commercial navigation, whether arising from armed attacks, piracy, geopolitical confrontation or institutional fragility, generate consequences that extend far beyond the immediate theatre of instability. Within this strategic environment, attempts to conceptualise Red Sea governance as the exclusive preserve of a select group of littoral states risk confusing territorial jurisdiction with the broader responsibilities of maritime security. Coastal states possess sovereign rights and jurisdiction recognised under international law; those rights must be respected. Yet sovereignty over territorial waters does not translate into an exclusive entitlement to determine the entire security architecture of a maritime corridor whose stability affects landlocked economies, international shipping and distant trading partners alike. Ethiopia’s case rests on precisely this distinction. Its geographical position, demographic scale, economic significance and dependence on maritime transit establish compelling grounds for substantive participation in regional deliberations concerning navigation, commercial resilience and maritime-security cooperation. Excluding Ethiopia from such arrangements would disregard the interconnected character of contemporary security, in which the vulnerabilities of one state can rapidly become the liabilities of an entire region. An effective Red Sea security order must therefore move beyond narrow geographical formalism towards a model of differentiated but shared responsibility. Littoral states would retain their sovereign prerogatives, while landlocked countries and other materially affected partners would contribute according to their capabilities, interests and agreed institutional mandates. Such an approach would neither diminish coastal sovereignty nor confer unilateral privileges upon Ethiopia. Rather, it would align the distribution of security responsibilities with the realities of regional interdependence. International Law and the Rights of Landlocked States International law provides an important foundation for this approach, although its provisions must be interpreted with precision. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) recognises the right of landlocked states to access to and from the sea for the purpose of exercising the rights conferred by the Convention. Part X further provides for freedom of transit through the territories of transit states, subject to mutually agreed terms and modalities. These provisions establish a legal basis for negotiated maritime access and transit arrangements; they do not, however, confer automatic rights to territorial sovereignty, a coastline or a naval presence in another state’s waters. The distinction is consequential. Ethiopia’s geographical circumstances do not extinguish its legitimate maritime interests, but the realisation of those interests must proceed through negotiated agreements, reciprocal commitments and respect for the sovereignty of coastal neighbours. Its objective should therefore be the institutionalisation of dependable access and meaningful participation in cooperative maritime security, rather than the assertion of unilateral legal entitlements unsupported by international law. UNCLOS also recognises the importance of cooperation in the management of semi-enclosed seas. Article 123 calls upon states bordering such seas to coordinate their activities and, where appropriate, to cooperate with other interested states and international organisations in matters including resource management, environmental protection and scientific research. Although this provision does not establish an unrestricted right to participate in every aspect of maritime governance, it reinforces the broader principle that the management of interconnected marine environments benefits from structured cooperation. For Ethiopia, these legal principles offer a constructive basis for diplomacy. Its substantial reliance on Red Sea trade gives it a compelling interest in the security of maritime approaches, the predictability of transit arrangements and the continuity of commercial navigation. The appropriate response is to translate that interest into durable bilateral and multilateral frameworks that recognise the rights of coastal states while ensuring that Ethiopia’s economic and security concerns receive institutional consideration. The governing principle should be straightforward: coastal sovereignty and the legitimate interests of landlocked states are not mutually exclusive; they must be reconciled through law, negotiation and reciprocal benefit. Precedents for Mutually Beneficial Maritime Access International practice demonstrates that geographical constraints need not condemn landlocked states to permanent logistical vulnerability. Across regions, governments have employed bilateral agreements, dedicated port facilities, transport corridors, customs arrangements and long-term commercial concessions to establish more predictable access to maritime trade. The 1965 boundary agreement between Jordan and Saudi Arabia, for example, reconfigured territory in the Gulf of Aqaba region and expanded Jordan’s coastline. Although rooted in a particular historical and territorial context, the agreement illustrates how negotiated settlements can reshape geographical constraints where the parties identify compatible strategic interests. It should not be treated as a template readily transferable to the Horn of Africa, but it demonstrates the possibilities and limitations of diplomacy in addressing questions of territorial access. A more directly applicable model lies in the development of transport and port corridors linking landlocked economies to coastal infrastructure. Arrangements associated with the Port of Nacala and Malawi illustrate how dedicated terminal capacity, improved rail and road connections, streamlined border procedures and coordinated logistics can generate reciprocal economic benefits. The coastal state gains transit revenue, investment and employment, while the landlocked partner obtains more reliable access to international markets. Comparable mechanisms could form the foundation of a more durable Ethiopia–coastal state partnership. Long-term port-utilisation agreements, dedicated terminal concessions, bonded logistics facilities, preferential commercial arrangements and integrated transport corridors could reduce Ethiopia’s exposure to logistical disruption while generating tangible economic returns for host countries. Where mutually acceptable, such agreements could incorporate joint investment, infrastructure development and coordinated security protocols. The essential consideration is reciprocity. Maritime access must not be framed as a zero-sum contest between Ethiopia and its coastal neighbours. Properly designed agreements can transform geographical proximity into a source of shared prosperity, giving coastal states a material interest in Ethiopia’s economic success while reducing the vulnerabilities associated with uncertain or excessively concentrated transit arrangements. Such arrangements would also provide a practical foundation for a more structured Ethiopian contribution to regional maritime security. Participation could include information-sharing, logistical assistance, coordinated threat assessments, capacity-building and other forms of cooperation negotiated with the relevant coastal authorities. Any naval deployment or operational presence would require an appropriate legal basis and the consent of the state concerned. These safeguards are not impediments to cooperation; they are the conditions that make it legitimate and sustainable. Historical Experience and Ethiopia’s Maritime Reorientation Ethiopia’s contemporary maritime predicament must also be understood in its historical context. Before Eritrea’s independence in 1993, Ethiopia possessed a coastline of approximately 700 kilometres and maintained a naval force with facilities associated with Massawa, Assab and the Dahlak Islands. Its maritime institutions formed part of a broader national security structure, connecting coastal defence, naval training and the protection of strategic approaches. The loss of direct access to the sea fundamentally altered Ethiopia’s strategic environment, but it did not eliminate the country’s dependence on maritime commerce. Nor did it diminish the regional consequences of instability along the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. The resulting asymmetry between Ethiopia’s continental economic significance and its dependence on infrastructure located beyond its sovereign territory remains a central feature of the country’s strategic calculations. Historical experience, however, should inform contemporary policy without dictating it. The restoration of Ethiopia’s maritime role cannot simply replicate the institutional arrangements of an earlier era, nor can historical possession of a coastline constitute a contemporary legal claim to territory belonging to another sovereign state. The circumstances of the region have changed, as have the legal and diplomatic conditions under which maritime cooperation must now operate. What remains relevant is the strategic lesson: a state whose prosperity depends heavily on maritime access has a compelling interest in the stability, predictability and security of the systems through which that access is exercised. Ethiopia’s long-term objective should therefore be to develop the economic, diplomatic and institutional capabilities necessary to protect its maritime interests through mutually agreed arrangements. The deterioration of security across parts of the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden makes this objective increasingly consequential. Threats to commercial shipping, attacks by armed non-state actors and the strategic competition surrounding vital maritime chokepoints expose the limitations of fragmented security responses. No single coastal administration, particularly one operating under substantial institutional and resource constraints, can be expected to neutralise every threat to a corridor of such international importance. Nevertheless, Ethiopia’s demographic and economic scale should not be mistaken for an automatic capacity to provide maritime security. Effective naval operations require specialised personnel, sustained financing, maritime surveillance, logistics, training, command structures and operational experience. A credible Ethiopian contribution would therefore require a carefully sequenced programme of institutional development, supported by diplomatic cooperation and realistic assessments of national resources. The strategic objective is not to substitute Ethiopian predominance for coastal-state authority. It is to ensure that Ethiopia’s substantial stake in the corridor is matched by an appropriate, lawful and operationally credible contribution to its security. Regional Security Contributions and Maritime Responsibility / Ethiopia’s record of involvement in regional security provides a relevant foundation for this endeavour. Its participation in African Union missions in Somalia, including sustained operations against Al-Shabaab, has demonstrated the extent to which its national security is intertwined with the stability of neighbouring states. Ethiopian diplomacy has also contributed to regional mediation efforts, including the 1972 Addis Ababa Agreement that ended the first Sudanese civil war and diplomatic engagement surrounding Sudan’s political transition in 2019. These experiences do not automatically establish a claim to maritime authority. They do, however, demonstrate that Ethiopia has substantial experience in security cooperation and a direct interest in preventing instability from spreading across the Horn of Africa. Extending that experience to maritime-security initiatives would be a logical development, provided it is guided by clear mandates, institutional preparedness and the consent of relevant partners. A modern Ethiopian maritime strategy should consequently integrate several mutually reinforcing priorities: dependable commercial access, diversified transit arrangements, maritime-domain awareness, cooperation against transnational threats and the development of specialised naval capabilities where economically and strategically justified. These objectives should be pursued incrementally, with an emphasis on professional competence, regional confidence-building and transparent legal arrangements. The wider Horn of Africa would benefit from an approach that treats maritime security as a shared regional public good rather than an instrument of geopolitical exclusion. Coastal states would retain control over their sovereign waters, while Ethiopia could contribute resources, expertise and institutional capacity to cooperative initiatives serving the interests of all participants. Such a framework would also reduce the risk that maritime access becomes a recurring source of bilateral tension. By embedding cooperation within durable agreements, the parties could replace episodic political bargaining with predictable mechanisms for resolving disputes, financing infrastructure and responding to emerging threats. The Strategic Case for International Engagement For international partners whose commercial prosperity depends on uninterrupted navigation through the Bab el-Mandeb and the southern Red Sea, an inclusive regional security architecture is a matter of practical strategic interest. The deployment of distant naval forces can provide important protection against immediate threats, but external intervention alone cannot substitute indefinitely for capable regional institutions, resilient transport networks and sustained political cooperation among neighbouring states. Ethiopia could become a more consequential contributor to this architecture, particularly through its diplomatic influence, economic weight and experience in regional security operations. Its participation would be most effective if embedded in a broader framework involving coastal governments, regional organisations and international partners, with clearly defined responsibilities and respect for the sovereignty of every participating state. International support should therefore prioritise the conditions that make cooperation viable: infrastructure investment, technical assistance, professional training, maritime information-sharing and the strengthening of regional mechanisms for crisis prevention. Any support for the development of Ethiopian naval capabilities should be assessed against clear objectives, available resources and the need to build confidence among neighbouring countries. The purpose of such engagement would not be to establish an Ethiopian sphere of influence over the Red Sea. It would be to create a more balanced distribution of responsibility for protecting a maritime corridor whose security is indispensable to regional development and global commerce. An Ethiopia that enjoys predictable maritime access, maintains constructive relations with coastal neighbours and contributes proportionately to regional security would offer international partners a more sustainable basis for cooperation than a regional order characterised by mistrust, fragmented responsibilities and recurring disputes over access. From Strategic Interest to a Durable Regional Order Ambassador Redwan Hussein’s remarks at the Tana High-Level Forum point towards a fundamental proposition: the security of the Red Sea must be organised around the realities of interdependence rather than the restrictive logic of geographical exclusion. The corridor’s importance to global commerce, coupled with the interconnected vulnerabilities of the Horn of Africa, makes inclusive cooperation a strategic necessity rather than a diplomatic courtesy. For Ethiopia, the implications are clear. Its maritime interests must be pursued through international law, negotiated access arrangements, sustained investment in national capabilities and a foreign policy that treats coastal neighbours as indispensable partners rather than obstacles to be overcome. For littoral states, a more engaged Ethiopia offers opportunities for infrastructure development, expanded trade, shared security initiatives and a broader distribution of the responsibilities associated with regional stability. The international community, meanwhile, has an interest in supporting arrangements that are both operationally effective and politically legitimate. A maritime security order that excludes a major regional economy risks leaving important vulnerabilities unaddressed; one that disregards coastal sovereignty would generate new sources of instability. The challenge is to construct an institutional framework capable of avoiding both extremes. Ultimately, the future of Red Sea security will depend less on assertions of exclusive entitlement than on the ability of regional states to reconcile legitimate national interests within a common strategic framework. Ethiopia’s case is strongest when grounded in that principle: not a demand for privileges beyond international law, but a compelling argument for meaningful participation commensurate with its economic exposure, regional responsibilities and capacity to contribute. The Red Sea is too strategically consequential to be governed through exclusion, and its security too interdependent to be sustained by fragmented responsibility. An inclusive, legally grounded and mutually beneficial maritime order one that respects coastal sovereignty while recognising the legitimate interests of landlocked states is therefore not merely desirable. It is essential to the long-term stability of the Horn of Africa and the uninterrupted functioning of one of the global economy’s most critical maritime arteries. Naval commanders and maritime representatives from Yemen, Oman, Djibouti, Somaliland and Puntland joined the Ethiopian Navy for a four day workshop on maritime search and rescue, information sharing and regional security. The meeting, which concludes on October 29, brought together authorities connected to some of the most strategically important coastlines in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. According to coverage of the Ethiopian National Defense Force announcement , the discussions aimed to strengthen coordination and improve responses to maritime emergencies. Beyond these immediate objectives, however, the gathering offers an opportunity to examine Ethiopia’s growing engagement with a region from which its geography has long separated it. Since Eritrea’s secession in 1993, Ethiopia has relied on neighboring countries for maritime access. This dependence carries considerable economic consequences. According to the World Bank , Djibouti handled approximately 95 percent of Ethiopian imports and exports at the time of its assessment, demonstrating the importance of a single corridor to the country’s external trade. Diversification through Berbera and other regional ports has therefore become increasingly important. Yet access to port infrastructure addresses only part of Ethiopia’s maritime concerns. The security of shipping routes, the reliability of regional partners and the institutions responsible for managing maritime emergencies also affect the country’s economic interests. The Addis Ababa meeting becomes particularly interesting when placed against the competing diplomatic arrangements emerging around the Red Sea. In January 2020, eight countries established the Council of Arab and African States Bordering the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden . Its members include Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan, Somalia, Djibouti, Yemen and Jordan. Membership was organized around coastal geography, leaving Ethiopia outside a forum concerned with the security of waters through which much of its international trade passes. This exclusion has acquired greater political significance as regional countries develop closer security relationships. On October 4, 2026, the leaders of Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan met in New Alamein and adopted a joint declaration affirming that Red Sea governance should remain the exclusive responsibility of littoral states. The declaration also rejected recognition of Somaliland and addressed disagreements concerning the Nile. These positions reveal an approach to regional governance that places significant emphasis on coastal sovereignty and territorial integrity. For Ethiopia, the challenge is clear. Its economic and security interests are tied to the Red Sea, yet some of the emerging regional arrangements provide no formal place for a landlocked country. The Addis Ababa workshop does not overturn these restrictions, nor does it establish a competing maritime alliance. It does, however, demonstrate that Ethiopia can engage coastal authorities through other forms of cooperation. Maritime governance is not confined to political councils; information sharing, emergency response and professional coordination also provide opportunities for meaningful participation. The composition of the gathering is particularly relevant in this respect. Djibouti remains Ethiopia’s principal gateway to international markets, making cooperation between the two countries essential to regional commerce. Somaliland, meanwhile, has become important to Ethiopia’s efforts to diversify its transport corridors through the development of Berbera port and its associated infrastructure . Puntland’s geographical position along the Gulf of Aden gives it an important role in maritime affairs near the approaches to the Indian Ocean. Their participation demonstrates that Ethiopia already maintains channels of communication with authorities responsible for maritime areas directly connected to its commercial interests. These relationships should not be mistaken for unconditional political support. Somaliland’s unresolved international status and Puntland’s disagreements with Somalia’s federal government introduce complications that cannot be ignored. In March 2024, Puntland announced that it would no longer recognize the authority of Somalia’s federal institutions following disputed constitutional amendments. Ethiopia’s own relations with Mogadishu were strained by the January 2024 memorandum of understanding with Somaliland, before the Ankara Declaration of December 2024 established a framework for pursuing mutually beneficial maritime arrangements while respecting Somalia’s sovereignty. Somalia’s federal government was notably absent from the list of participants, although it remains unclear whether Mogadishu was invited. Still, Ethiopia’s engagement with Somaliland and Puntland does not necessarily have to come at the expense of its relations with Somalia. Addis Ababa has an interest in maintaining ties with all three, particularly given their importance to security along the Gulf of Aden. The challenge will be to strengthen these relationships without deepening existing political disagreements. The participation of Yemen and Oman extends the meeting’s relevance beyond the Horn of Africa. Yemen occupies a critical position near Bab al Mandeb, where instability can disrupt shipping between the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea. However, Yemen’s internal fragmentation limits what cooperation with its internationally recognized authorities can accomplish. As a 2026 British parliamentary assessment explains, the Houthi movement controls much of northwestern Yemen and has expanded its influence along parts of the Red Sea coastline. Oman brings a different perspective through its position along the Arabian Peninsula and its connections to the wider Indian Ocean. For Ethiopia, engagement with these authorities offers opportunities for communication, maritime safety cooperation and professional exchanges. It does not guarantee their support for Ethiopian naval basing or sea access negotiations. Nevertheless, regular contact can help build the confidence required for more substantial agreements. Relationships established around less contentious matters may eventually support discussions on broader economic and security interests. The meeting also forms part of an established international framework rather than an exclusively Ethiopian initiative. As reports on the workshop indicate, the event is associated with the European Union supported Crisis Response Project for the Red Sea and Western Indian Ocean, alongside CRIMARIO and Expertise France. These initiatives emphasize maritime awareness, information sharing and improved coordination. Ethiopia’s contribution lies in hosting regional representatives and participating in a wider system of cooperation supported by international partners. Importantly, Ethiopia’s involvement in maritime security predates the current meeting. The country was among the original signatories of the Djibouti Code of Conduct in 2009 , which established a framework for cooperation against piracy and armed robbery at sea. More recently, an International Maritime Organization workshop held in Addis Ababa in August 2026 produced a roadmap for establishing a National Maritime Information Sharing Centre. The proposed institution would improve coordination among Ethiopian agencies and strengthen their connections to regional maritime information networks. This is perhaps the clearest evidence of practical progress. A functioning information sharing centre could help Ethiopia monitor developments affecting its commercial interests, coordinate responses to maritime incidents and maintain contact with regional partners. Such capabilities would not resolve the logistical difficulties of operating a navy without a sovereign coastline. Naval deployment still requires access to suitable ports, maintenance facilities and operational infrastructure. Nevertheless, institutional capacity and diplomatic relationships are necessary components of any credible maritime strategy. Ethiopia’s interest in the Red Sea should therefore be understood through both its ambitions and its existing opportunities. The country has legitimate economic reasons to seek dependable maritime access, while neighboring states have their own sovereignty and security concerns. Cooperation offers a means of pursuing these interests without treating them as necessarily incompatible. Ethiopia’s commercial demand, transport infrastructure and regional relationships can provide incentives for arrangements that also benefit coastal partners. For Ethiopia, this is an encouraging beginning. Its maritime future cannot rest solely on negotiations over a particular port or coastline. It will also be shaped by the relationships it builds with neighboring countries and its contribution to the security of the region. The lasting impact of the October gathering remains to be seen, but its immediate significance should not be dismissed. In a region where competing political interests often dominate discussions of the Red Sea, cooperation offers Ethiopia an additional path through which to advance its economic interests, strengthen diplomatic relationships and establish a more enduring role in regional maritime affairs. Sudan’s military, which has been fighting the RSF since April 2023, has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of aiding the paramilitary group, including by allowing drone attacks from Ethiopian territory. Ethiopia denies the accusations and has in turn accused the Sudanese army of backing rebels linked to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which Khartoum rejects. In a statement on Sunday, Sudan’s army-aligned foreign ministry accused Ethiopia of “blatant aggression” in its formal complaints to the Security Council and the AU Peace and Security Council. “The use of Ethiopian territory by the terrorist militia (RSF) to target Sudanese territory is considered a hostile act that places Ethiopia in violation of international law,” it said. In a report on Sunday, Sudan’s army-led Transitional Sovereignty Council said it had documented 70 attacks this year involving 187 one-way attack drones launched from Ethiopian territory, killing or wounding nearly 500 civilians. It said the attacks targeted residential complexes, hospitals and power and fuel stations. Both the army and the RSF have increasingly relied on drones that can strike targets hundreds of kilometers away without putting their fighters at risk. More than 1,100 people were killed in drone attacks across Sudan in the first half of the year, according to the United Nations. Recent attacks on power stations in army-controlled areas have caused widespread power cuts in Khartoum, Al-Jazirah, White Nile and Gedaref states. — AFP LAST UPDATE: November 02, 2026 01:43 PM Share Share Options Copy Link Email Facebook Twitter Telegram LinkedIn Whatsapp Opinion If we are always connected, why do we feel alone? somalia.content: Pirates hijack Iranian fishing vessel off Somalia’s northeastern coast - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Pirates hijack Iranian fishing vessel off Somalia’s northeastern coast Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Monday November 2, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) – Armed pirates have hijacked an Iranian fishing vessel off Somalia’s northeastern coast, raising concerns that it could be used as a mothership to launch attacks on larger commercial ships. The European Union Naval Force’s Maritime Security Centre Indian Ocean (MSCIO) said the pirates boarded the vessel, named Azini, at around 0900 UTC near coordinates 09°42’N, 053°55’E, approximately 185 nautical miles east of Bandarbayla, Somalia. The safety of the crew remained unknown. An officer with Puntland’s maritime police told The Associated Press that 12 pirates had seized the vessel and its 23 crew members, including 21 Iranian fishermen and two Somali security guards. MSCIO said the Azini matched the profile of vessels Somali pirates have previously used as motherships. Such vessels provide pirates with mobile bases from which to launch attacks on larger merchant ships farther offshore, beyond the operating range of smaller speedboats. By Saturday, the vessel had moved approximately 110 nautical miles farther east to coordinates 09°47’N, 055°45’E, bringing it closer to a major commercial shipping route. MSCIO reiterated its warning that the fishing vessel could be used as a pirate mothership. The hijacking comes amid renewed concerns over piracy off Somalia, following several years of relative calm. In August 2026, Turkish naval forces and the Somali National Armed Forces rescued the cargo vessel MV LATUF after it was hijacked off the Somali coast, according to Somalia’s Defence Ministry. The ministry said four boats used by the pirates were destroyed and 14 pirates were killed during the joint operation. It added that sustained pressure from security forces forced the remaining pirates to abandon the vessel. Security forces subsequently took control of the ship, which resumed its voyage safely, the ministry said. The operation was conducted under a defence cooperation agreement between Somalia and Türkiye, which provides a framework for cooperation in protecting Somalia’s coastline and combating maritime piracy. Somalia experienced a major wave of piracy between 2008 and 2018, with armed groups targeting commercial vessels and demanding ransoms. Attacks declined significantly for several years before re-emerging in late 2023 amid heightened security tensions in the region. Make New York Post a Preferred Source Ilhan Omar has been hiding links to two of her siblings in London in an alleged bid to create further distance between her and rumored brother Ahmed Nur Said Elmi — whom she married in 2009. Multiple sources told The Post that Mohamed Nur Said Elmi, a political activist for the Puntland cause in Somalia, and Leila Nur Said Elmi, 53, are Omar’s siblings who live in London. Ahmed Elmi, 41 — to whom Omar was married for eight years, and who described himself as “a gay man” in a recent academic paper — is also believed to have lived with Leila while growing up. 9 Ilhan Omar has been hiding links to London siblings Mohamed Nur and Leila Nur, above, in an alleged bid to create further distance between her and rumored brother Ahmed Nur Said Elmi — whom she married in 2009. Business Insider Edition United States International Deutschland & Österreich España Japan México Nederland Polska ADVERTISEMENT BI Africa > local > markets Despite warnings from China, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, Israel presses ahead with embassy plans in breakaway African territory near Red Sea Olamilekan Okebiorun 02 November 2026 10:31 PM Israel is moving ahead with plans to establish an embassy in Somaliland despite opposition from China, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkey and Somalia, adding to the list of powerful countries vying for influence in the strategically important Red Sea region. China and Saudi Arabia opposed Israel’s recognition of Somaliland in December 2025, citing Somalia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Photo credit: BIA Israel is proceeding with plans to open an embassy in Somaliland despite strong opposition from China, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkey, and Somalia. Somaliland, self-governed since 1991 but lacking broad international recognition, holds strategic significance due to its location near the Red Sea and important shipping lanes. The US upholds Israel's right to establish diplomatic relations but has not recognized Somaliland's independence, maintaining its support for Somalia's territorial integrity. China, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Turkey have condemned Israel's actions, citing violations of Somalia's sovereignty and warning of regional destabilization. ADVERTISEMENT Read Also markets Top 10 African countries with the lowest fuel prices in October 2026 markets Top 10 African countries with the lowest debt to the IMF in October 2026 markets Top 10 African countries with the strongest currencies in October 2026 On November 1, 2026, Israel's Foreign Ministry confirmed that its first ambassador to Somaliland, Michael Lotem, had presented his credentials to President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi in Hargeisa, the territory's capital, where officials also laid the cornerstone for the planned embassy. The move follows Israel's recognition of Somaliland on December 26, 2025, making it the first United Nations member state to recognise the territory since it declared independence from Somalia in 1991. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar reaffirmed the country's commitment, stating, "Israel is determined to develop and strengthen its relations with Somaliland." ADVERTISEMENT Plans for the embassy have been underway for months, with Israel appointing Lotem, its former ambassador to Kenya, as its first envoy to Somaliland in April 2026, before Somaliland's ambassador to Israel, Mohamed Hagi, presented his credentials in May. Relations strengthened further in June when Somaliland opened its first embassy in Jerusalem during President Abdullahi's visit to Israel, marking another step towards formalising diplomatic ties. DON'T MISS: Two Chinese mining firms pull out of Kenya’s rare earth and niobium extraction race as three American companies stand their ground among five remaining bidders Why Somaliland matters to Israel Somaliland has governed itself since separating from Somalia in 1991, but limited international recognition has restricted its access to global institutions, development financing and diplomatic representation. ADVERTISEMENT Its strategic location along the Gulf of Aden, near the Red Sea, has attracted international interest, with the UAE-developed port of Berbera lying 160 miles from Yemen, near a major shipping route where Iranian-backed Houthi rebels have attacked commercial vessels. President Abdullahi highlighted the importance of the relationship, saying, "Given our strategic position around the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, our cooperation carries important regional and international significance." China, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Turkey reject recognition However, Israel's embassy plans and earlier recognition of Somaliland have drawn strong opposition from China, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Egypt, which support Somalia's sovereignty and territorial integrity and have strategic interests in the Red Sea region. On December 29, 2025, China condemned Israel's recognition of Somaliland, warning against foreign interference in Somalia's internal affairs. ADVERTISEMENT Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said, "No country should encourage or support other countries' internal separatist forces for its own selfish interests." Beijing also raised the issue at the United Nations Security Council, where its deputy permanent representative, Sun Lei, urged Israel to reverse its decision, warning that the recognition could further destabilise the Horn of Africa. Saudi Arabia similarly reaffirmed its "full support for Somalia's sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity" following Israel's announcement in December 2025. Egypt reinforced its opposition on January 8, 2026, when Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty warned that Israel's recognition could destabilise the Horn of Africa and the wider region. "This is a dangerous precedent that threatens peace, security, and stability at the regional and international levels," Abdelatty said. ADVERTISEMENT In April, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Turkey and other countries jointly condemned Israel's appointment of a diplomatic representative to Somaliland, describing it as a "flagrant violation" of Somalia's sovereignty. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan had earlier rejected the recognition during a meeting with Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud. "The preservation of Somalia's unity and integrity under any circumstances is a priority for us. Israel's decision to recognize Somaliland is illegitimate and unacceptable," Erdoğan said. US maintains its position on Somalia The United States, Israel's closest ally, has continued to defend its right to establish diplomatic relations with Somaliland, despite opposition from other countries, but has stopped short of recognising the territory's independence. ADVERTISEMENT At a December 2025 UN Security Council meeting, US Deputy Ambassador Tammy Bruce said, "Israel has the same right to conduct diplomatic relations as any other sovereign state." However, Washington maintained that its position on Somaliland remained unchanged. "We have no announcement to make regarding U.S. recognition of Somaliland. And there has been no change in American policy," Bruce added. Somalia, meanwhile, continues to reject Israel's recognition, insisting that Somaliland remains "an integral, inseparable, and inalienable part" of its sovereign territory. EST | Ayang Macdonald Categories Biometrics News | Civil / National ID | ID for All Somalia’s National Identification and Registration Authority (NIRA) has announced the implementation of Hubiye, its national ID verification platform, as the country expands the use of digital identity across banking and public services. The system enables participating institutions to check identity credentials against NIRA’s national database. The ID authority announced the development towards the end of October in a post on its Facebook page, stating: “NIRA has implemented the Hubiye system which facilitates the verification of the authenticity of identity credentials by service providers while also enforcing legal procedures to safeguard the security of citizens’ data.” Hubiye is one of three foundational digital public infrastructure systems launched by NIRA in May last year, alongside the Certificate Delivery System (CDS) and the eAqoonsi app. The latter provides citizens with a digital version of their national ID, which authorities are encouraging them to use to access services. The operationalization of Hubiye comes as Somalia moves from building a national ID database towards making the national ID a functional layer of its digital public infrastructure. A service provider initiates verification by submitting an applicant’s national ID number to Hubiye. The system sends a one-time password by SMS or email to the ID holder, who supplies it to the provider to authorize verification against NIRA’s database. In April last year, the Somali government directed public-facing service providers to integrate with Hubiye to facilitate identity verification and access to services. While integration with the platform is initially free, NIRA says certain service providers may eventually pay for access. UNDP reported in May 2026 that Hubiye supported real-time identity verification across 25 integrated services, including commercial banking, with the system serving approximately 1.2 million citizens. Hubiye’s implementation also supports Somalia’s broader digital government plans, including Halmeel, a unified public service delivery platform established by a Cabinet resolution in April. In an interview with Biometric Update last month , Halmeel Director General Mohamed Dubo said the platform is expected to launch by the end of March 2027, with plans to initially integrate about 70 government services. He noted that the platform depends on NIRA, as the national ID is the only accepted identification credential at Halmeel’s physical service centres. NIRA is a principal partner in the initiative, and the two institutions are working to integrate their systems. These developments are part of the Somali government’s ongoing efforts to consolidate its digital public infrastructure and advance digital transformation, with the national ID serving as the foundation for the wider service-delivery ecosystem. NIRA has set a target of enrolling at least 15 million people in its national ID system by 2029, as authorities seek to expand its use across public and private sector services. The agreement was signed in Djibouti City by the Speaker of Somalia's House of the People, Abdoulkadir Mohamed Nour ‘Jaamac’ and the President of Djibouti's National Assembly, Dileita Mohamed Dileita. The memorandum establishes a framework for expanding cooperation between the two legislative bodies, with a focus on sharing expertise, exchanging institutional experience and developing partnerships. Under the agreement, the two sides intend to cooperate on improving legislative processes, strengthening the professional skills of parliamentary staff, organising training programmes, conducting legal research and modernising parliamentary working procedures. مشدداً في الوقت ذاته على احترام فريقه للبطولة الخليجية، مع تمسكه بأولوية المنافسة على لقب الدوري المحلي. وأوضح بلماضي، خلال المؤتمر الصحافي الذي يسبق المواجهة، أن ضيق الفترة الزمنية بين المباريات صعّب عملية التحضير، وقال: «استعدادنا لهذه المباراة كان نوعاً ما صعباً، لعبنا مباراة أمام الوكرة في الدوري قبل يومين، وكانت التدريبات فقط استرجاعية واستشفائية». وفي رده على سؤال «الشرق الأوسط» بشأن موقفه من الدفع بالتشكيلة الأساسية أمام نيوم، في ظل تصدر الدحيل مجموعته في البطولة الخليجية ومنافسته على صدارة الدوري القطري مناصفة مع السد والريان، إلى جانب اقتراب مواجهته المرتقبة أمام الغرافة، أكد بلماضي أن فريقه لن يتعامل مع الاستحقاق الخليجي باعتباره مباراة هامشية، موضحاً أن الاختيارات ستخضع لاحتياجات المواجهة. وقال: «نحترم بطولة الخليج، وهدفنا الأول تحقيق الدوري، وهذا هدف الإدارة أيضاً. غداً سندخل بالتشكيلة المناسبة، وسنفكر في مباراة الغرافة لاحقاً». من جانبه، استعاد اللاعب القطري مبارك شنّان، لاعب الدحيل، ذكرياته مع الفرنسي كريستوف غالتييه مدرب نيوم، قبل المواجهة المرتقبة بين الفريقين، معبّراً عن تقديره للفترة التي جمعتهما، ومؤكداً تطلعه إلى ظهور فريقه بصورة تليق بطموحاته. وقال شنّان: «عشنا ذكريات جيدة مع المدرب غالتييه، وغداً نتواجه، ونتمنى التوفيق لفريق الدحيل». كما وجّه لاعب الدحيل الشكر إلى أهالي تبوك على حفاوة الاستقبال، مؤكداً أن فريقه يتطلع إلى المنافسة على اللقب، وقال: «نشكركم على حفاوة الاستقبال في تبوك، وهدفنا تحقيق البطولة، وسنظهر بمستوى لائق غداً بمشيئة الله». وتحمل المواجهة أفريقيا . كما استعاد المهاجم أداما كوليبالي مكانه في صفوف الفريق بتوقيت مثالي، قبل خوض المنافسات الأفريقية، ليمنح زينباور إضافة نوعية، باعتباره أحد الركائز الأساسية التي أسهمت في الطفرة التي حققها football.content: خلافات تهدد مشروع أبياه مع المنتخب السوداني.. والرحيل يلوح في الأفق — تاق برس اعجاب المتابعين الثلاثاء, نوفمبر 3, 2026 من نحن السياسة التحريرية للإعلان على تاق برس اتصل بنا تاق برس - اخبار السودان والعالم الرئيسية أخبار عاجلة سياسية منوعات وثقافة إقتصاد رياضة علوم وتكنلوجيا مقالات أخري تقارير صحة الرئيسية أخبار رياضة خلافات تهدد مشروع أبياه مع المنتخب السوداني.. والرحيل يلوح في الأفق خلافات تهدد مشروع أبياه مع المنتخب السوداني.. والرحيل يلوح في الأفق بواسطة editor في أكتوبر 31, 2026 238 مشاركة متابعات تاق برس – تتجه العلاقة بين الغاني كواسي أبياه، المدير الفني للمنتخب الوطني السوداني الأول، والاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم نحو منعطف بالغ الخطورة، في ظل تصاعد الضغوط والتدخلات التي باتت تحاصر المدرب، وتضع تجربته مع صقور الجديان على المحك، وسط مؤشرات متزايدة على اقتراب نهاية مشواره مع المنتخب. وتشير المعلومات التي تحصل عليها “الترا سودان” من داخل مجلس إدارة الاتحاد إلى أن أبياه بات يشعر بأن ما يتعرض له يمثل تحركات منظمة تستهدف تقويض صلاحياته وإضعاف موقفه، تمهيداً لإبعاده عن قيادة المنتخب. وهو ما أسرّ به لعدد من المقربين منه، معبّراً عن استيائه الشديد من الأجواء التي يعمل فيها. وبحسب المعلومات ذاتها، فإن المدرب الغاني بات يعتقد أن هناك مخططاً يُحاك ضده، وأن بعض القرارات والتوجهات الأخيرة داخل الاتحاد لا يمكن فصلها عن مساعٍ لإجباره على مغادرة موقعه، بعدما وجد نفسه في مواجهة تدخلات متكررة في صميم اختصاصاته الفنية. التغييرات التي طالت الجهازين الإداري والفني المساعد لم تكن أمراً عابراً بالنسبة للمدرب الغاني، خصوصاً بعد إبعاد المدير الإداري أبوبكر الماحي، وابتعاد المدرب العام صلاح الفنج عن موقعه ضمن المنظومة التي عملت معه خلال الفترة الماضية. ويمثل الرجلان عنصرين مهمين في منظومة أبياه، وكان المدرب ينظر إليهما باعتبارهما من ركائز الاستقرار داخل المنتخب، الأمر الذي دفعه إلى المطالبة بإعادة ترتيب الأوضاع بما يضمن عودة الانسجام إلى الجهازين الفني والإداري. لكن ما حدث عزز شعوره بأن هناك توجهاً لإعادة تشكيل المنظومة المحيطة به، دون اعتبار لرؤيته أو احتياجاته، وبكوادر لا تمتلك بالضرورة الخبرة المطلوبة للعمل في منتخب بحجم صقور الجديان. ومن أكثر الملفات التي أثارت غضب أبياه الضغوط المتواصلة بشأن إبعاد عدد من أصحاب الخبرة والعناصر الأساسية التي شكلت العمود الفقري للمنتخب خلال مشواره الأخير. فالمدرب الغاني لا يرى مبرراً للتخلي عن عناصر أثبتت جدارتها وقدمت الكثير للمنتخب، لمجرد ارتباط بعضها بملف المطالبة بالمستحقات المالية. كما لا يخفي تحفظاته على محاولات فرض أسماء جديدة ضمن القائمة، دون أن تكون هناك قناعة فنية مكتملة بشأن قدراتها. وتفاقمت الأزمة مع التوجه نحو تغيير نسبة من قوام المنتخب وإقحام عناصر من منتخب الشباب، في وقت يرى فيه أبياه أن الإحلال والتجديد لا ينبغي أن يتحولا إلى قرارات فوقية تتجاوز التقييم الفني واحتياجات المنتخب. ولم تتوقف مصادر الإحباط عند التدخل في اختيار اللاعبين وإدارة الجهاز الفني، بل امتدت إلى عدم تنفيذ عدد من البرامج الإعدادية التي اقترحها المدرب، وفي مقدمتها إقامة معسكر مبكر عقب فراغ الهلال والمريخ من مشاركتهما في البطولات الأفريقية. وكان أبياه يعوّل على الاستفادة من تلك الفترة في تجهيز المنتخب بصورة مثالية، والاستفادة من وجود العناصر الأساسية في السودان. غير أن عدم الاستجابة للمقترح أضاف حلقة جديدة إلى سلسلة الخلافات بينه والاتحاد. وبدا للمدرب أن برامجه وتصوراته لا تجد الاهتمام المطلوب، وأنه مطالب بتحقيق النتائج وتحمل المسؤولية كاملة، دون أن تتوفر له الظروف والصلاحيات اللازمة. التطور الأكثر إثارة في هذه الأزمة أن أبياه، وفقاً للمعلومات التي تحصلت عليها مصادرنا، لمح للمقربين منه بأن مواجهتي المنتخب أمام السنغال ذهاباً وإياباً قد تكونان آخر مشاويره مع صقور الجديان. وتشير هذه المعطيات إلى أن المدرب الغاني بدأ بالفعل التفكير في وضع حد لتجربته عقب المباراتين، في ظل قناعته بأن الأجواء الحالية لم تعد تساعده على مواصلة العمل بالصورة التي يريدها، وأن حجم التدخلات والضغوط تجاوز الحدود التي يمكن التعايش معها. وإذا مضى أبياه في هذا الاتجاه، فإن المنتخب الوطني سيكون أمام خسارة مدرب كبير قاده إلى مرحلة مميزة من النتائج والإنجازات، في وقت يحتاج فيه إلى الاستقرار والاستمرارية أكثر من حاجته إلى الدخول في مغامرة فنية وإدارية جديدة. ما يحدث الآن يتجاوز خلافاً حول قائمة أو لاعب أو معسكر إعدادي. نحن أمام أزمة ثقة تتسع يوماً بعد يوم، ومدرب بات يشعر بأنه مستهدف، وأن هناك من يعمل على إضعاف تجربته وإفقاده أدوات النجاح، قبل أن يصبح رحيله أمراً واقعاً. والسؤال الذي ينبغي أن يجيب عنه الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم ليس ما إذا كان أبياه سيغادر فحسب، بل من يتحمل مسؤولية الوصول بعلاقة المنتخب مع مدرب صنع معه إنجازات كبيرة إلى هذه المرحلة؟ هل هناك مشروع فني بديل يستحق التضحية بتجربة أبياه؟ أم أن صقور الجديان يدفعون ثمن صراعات وتدخلات إدارية لا علاقة لها بمصلحة المنتخب؟ المؤكد أن خسارة أبياه، إن حدثت بالطريقة التي تلوح في الأفق، ستكون بداية هدم مشروع كان يستحق الحماية والاستقرار والبناء عليه. اتحاد كرة القدم صقور الجديان كواسي أبياه 238 مشاركة أخبار ذات صلة رياضة أبياه يعلن القائمة الأولية لصقور
